narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three pieces of information, ranked by importance. First, your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor. You placed in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low ranking strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure.

Second, your LSAT score of 33 worked in your favor. It was the next most influential detail and pulled the prediction back toward passing, though not enough to overcome the other factors.

Third, your first-year class ranking also mattered. Like your third-year rank, you again placed in the bottom decile, well below the average sixth-decile performance of accepted students. This further increased the model’s estimate of your risk of failing the bar.

Taken together, your consistently low class standings outweighed the positive signal from your LSAT and led the system to conclude you were more likely than not to fail the bar exam.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on raising your academic performance to the middle or upper ranks of your class. Stronger grades in the coming year, combined with a higher LSAT retake if possible, would substantially improve your profile for future applications.
